Reward encoding in mPFC GCaMP signals

Two complementary GLMs — a time-resolved encoding model and a continuous FIR deconvolution model — run on the corrected, MATLAB-verified “none” (no DCZ/saline) cohort.

Summary

A clean, reward-locked signal emerges once alignment is fixed

Both pooled models agree on the same core finding: reward delivery drives a large, sharply-timed change in the mPFC photometry signal right at side-port entry, on top of a slower background modulation by recent reward history. The two approaches were fit independently, on the same data, using unrelated statistical machinery (per-timepoint OLS vs. ridge-regularized deconvolution) — their agreement is itself evidence that the effect is real rather than a modeling artifact. A separate set of within-animal analyses (below) tests this more specifically using each mouse's own fitted decision-value model, and confirms a value-dependent, outcome-locked modulation in all 7 mice individually — though not every pre-specified test in that set came back confirmatory, reported as run.

Headline result. The Reward coefficient in the encoding model steps sharply from ~0 to −1.2 (β per SD) exactly at side-port entry and holds there — not a gradual drift, a step. The FIR model's 8 reward-history kernels separate cleanly by recent outcome, with sessions following recent losses sitting far above sessions following recent wins.

Data & validation

What went into this analysis

All 38 sessions passed a fresh QC pass (sync quality, behavioral engagement, signal range) and were processed with a per-session hemisphere assignment — this cohort's rig underwent a mid-June-2023 channel cutover where every mouse's active fluorescence channel switched sides, so hemisphere could not be treated as a fixed per-mouse property. Trial-to-photometry alignment and the dF/F/z-score computation were independently verified against the lab's original MATLAB pipeline output for a reference session: resolved event indices matched to within 1 sample, and the z-scored trace matched MATLAB's own output at correlation 1.000000.

Model 1 — Time-resolved encoding GLM

A regression at every timepoint around side-port entry

An independent OLS regression was fit at each sample from −2.16 s to +5.4 s around side-port entry, predicting the trial-level z-scored signal from choice, reward, reward history, decision-value strength, and behavioral state. Numeric predictors were standardized, so each β is in units of signal change per 1 SD of that predictor.

Z ~ Choice * Reward + Reward_lag1 + Reward_lag2 + Reward_lag3 + Q_diff_abs + C(Behavioral_State)

Reading the panels

  • Reward — steps from ~0 to −1.2 exactly at t=0 and stays there. The single largest, most sharply-timed effect in the model.
  • Model fit — R² sits low and flat before the event (~0.04–0.06, as it should: behavior can't predict a neural response to an outcome that hasn't happened yet), then rises sharply right after t=0 to a peak of ~0.20, decaying gradually over the following seconds as the acute response fades.
  • Reward_lag1 / lag2 / lag3 — smooth, monotonically increasing ramps spanning the whole window with no discontinuity at t=0, consistent with a slowly-accumulating history/value signal rather than an event-locked response.
  • Choice and Choice:Reward — smaller, well-timed deviations around the event; the interaction term indicates the reward effect is modulated somewhat by which side was chosen.
  • Behavioral_State terms (Exploration, Left Bias, Right Bias) — clear post-event deviations from the Exploitation baseline, widest confidence bands on Left/Right Bias reflecting fewer trials in those states.
  • Q_diff_abs — noisier; a pre-event dip with partial recovery after, the weakest-powered term in the model.
Model 2 — FIR deconvolution GLM

Deconvolving the continuous trace directly

Rather than averaging pre-cut windows, this model regresses the full continuous z-scored session trace against time-shifted impulse regressors anchored at side-port entry, one 39-bin (±1.0 s) kernel per 3-trial reward-history pattern (reward_seq_3, most-recent-trial-first), plus parametric modulation by |Q difference| and choice side. Because every history group's kernel is fit jointly against the same trace, temporally overlapping trials — e.g. quick back-to-back win-stay sequences — are deconvolved from one another rather than confounded. Regularization strength was chosen by RidgeCV; out-of-sample performance was assessed with 10-fold GroupShuffleSplit cross-validation, grouped by trial so no trial's samples appear in both train and test.

Reading the panels

  • Ordering by history — the 8 patterns separate cleanly by baseline level: patterns with more recent losses (000, 001, 100) sit at a high positive baseline (~0.4–0.7); patterns with more recent wins (110, 111) sit at a negative baseline (~−0.3 to −0.4). Every group shares the same underlying shape, just offset by history.
  • Shared shape — a dip in the second or so before side-in, a rebound peak shortly after, then decay back toward baseline by +1 s.
  • Side In × |Q diff| and Side In × Choice — smaller-amplitude modulations layered on top, both showing structure around the event rather than flat noise.

Within-animal analyses

The pre-specified confirmatory tests, at the animal level

Everything above is pooled across sessions. The four analyses below are the pre-specified tests run separately within each of the 7 mice — one estimate per animal, compared across animals with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test rather than averaged — using trial-level model RPE derived from each animal's own sticky-Q fit (RPE_signed = outcome − Q(chosen action), using the pre-outcome value the fitted model assigns to the option actually chosen). Reported plainly, including where a test did not confirm the hypothesis.

1. Within-animal RPE regression

Post-event amplitude (mean z-score, 0–1 s after side-port entry) regressed on RPE_signed alone, separately per mouse.

All 7 mice show a significant negative βRPE (range −0.56 to −0.95, each individually p < 5×10−6); Wilcoxon across the 7 mice, p=0.016 — the strongest possible result obtainable at n=7. But the single-predictor RPE model explains modest variance (R²=0.016–0.043 per mouse) — in fact less than outcome alone explains in every mouse (R²=0.027–0.079). Since RPE_signed is mathematically a constrained version of outcome + Q(chosen) (equal-and-opposite coefficients forced), this says the simple textbook RPE formula isn't the best-fitting shape of the effect here. What is uniformly clean: letting outcome and value have independent, freely-fit coefficients (outcome × Q(chosen) interaction) shows a negative, significant interaction term in 7/7 mice (p from 0.018 to 1.2×10−10) — higher expected value of the chosen option consistently dampens the reward response, in every single animal, even if the exact functional form differs from a simple linear RPE.

2. Temporal specificity: does the value modulation appear before the event too?

The interaction above was fit again with pre_amp (mean z-score, −1 to 0 s before side-port entry) as the outcome, per mouse — a temporal control: a real outcome-locked effect should vanish before the outcome exists to reflect.

It vanishes cleanly. Post-event: significant in 7/7 mice, uniformly negative. Pre-event: significant in 0/7 mice (all p > 0.30, most > 0.5), and the sign isn't even consistent across animals (3 negative, 4 positive, all near zero). This is a real within-animal temporal control, not a pooled average: the value modulation is specific to the outcome window in every single mouse, supporting an outcome-locked signal rather than a standing pre-decision value representation that happens to also be visible afterward.

3. Signed vs. unsigned RPE

5-fold cross-validated out-of-sample R², per mouse, comparing post_amp ~ RPE_signed + Q_diff_abs + choice_side against the same model with RPE_signed replaced by |RPE|.

This one does not confirm. Only 4/7 mice show signed beating unsigned; Wilcoxon p=0.22 — not significant. Despite Analysis 1's clean, uniform result for the signed regression itself, this specific head-to-head comparison doesn't establish that sign information reliably beats magnitude-only encoding at the group level in this dataset. Reported as run, not adjusted or re-specified after seeing the result.

4. Between-animal variability of the two pooled models

Both GLMs refit separately per mouse, from the same extracted data (no raw reprocessing) — encoding-model peak R² and FIR out-of-sample R², one point per animal.

Real variability, and the pooled estimate isn't a distortion of it: encoding-model peak R² ranges 0.152–0.325, with the pooled ~0.20 sitting inside that spread, not at either extreme. FIR out-of-sample R² is more variable (0.048–0.292), and the two weakest fits (WCL25, WCL26) are also the two mice with the fewest sessions (2 each, vs. 5–8 for the rest) — a genuine confound this analysis can't resolve: it may be real biological variability, or simply less reliable estimation from less data per animal.

Interpretation

What the evidence, taken together, supports

Two structurally different pooled models — a per-timepoint linear regression and a continuous-trace deconvolution, fit with unrelated regularization/cross-validation machinery — converge on the same reward-locked signal. The within-animal analyses add a more specific claim: a value-dependent modulation of that response (higher expected value of the chosen option → smaller response) that is consistent in direction across all 7 mice and specific to the post-outcome window in all 7 mice, absent beforehand. That combination — consistent sign across animals, and a clean temporal dissociation within each animal — is stronger, more specific evidence than either the pooled models or a single within-animal test in isolation.

What's not established: that the modulation takes the precise linear, equal-and-opposite shape the textbook signed-RPE formula assumes (the constrained RPE model underperforms the freely-fit interaction in every mouse), or that sign information reliably outperforms magnitude-only encoding in a direct model comparison (Analysis 3, n.s.). The evidence supports value modulates the outcome response, in a consistent direction, specific to the outcome period more strongly than it supports the specific claim this is a linear signed prediction-error signal.

Scope. This covers only the “none” (no DCZ/saline) condition. Pooled peak/out-of-sample R² values (~0.18–0.20) reflect single-trial-level prediction of a noisy bulk-fluorescence signal from a handful of behavioral regressors — a respectable effect size for this kind of analysis, not a claim that these variables explain most of the signal's variance. The encoding model's pooled β values are per-SD-of-standardized-predictor, not raw rewarded-minus-unrewarded differences in z-score units. Between-animal R² variability (Analysis 4) is confounded with per-animal trial count and cannot yet be attributed to biology vs. statistical power.
